nameStory: The Multicolored Bark Crab Spider gets its name from its remarkable ability to change colors to match tree bark, shifting between shades of brown, gray, and even white. Like other crab spiders, it holds its front legs wide like a crab's claws, ready to grab unsuspecting prey. The 'multicolored' part of its name reflects this chameleon-like talent that makes it a master of disguise.
description: The Multicolored Bark Crab Spider is a compact, robust spider that specializes in hunting on tree bark. It has a wide, flattened body with legs that extend sideways rather than forward, giving it that characteristic crab-like appearance. This spider is a medium-sized crab spider, typically reaching about 8-10mm in body length. Its most remarkable feature is its ability to change colors to perfectly blend with whatever bark surface it's hunting on.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Wide, flattened body with a distinctly crab-like posture - the front two pairs of legs extend sideways and are noticeably longer and more robust than the back legs

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Variable coloration that can shift from mottled brown and gray to nearly white, often with subtle darker chevron or angular patterns that mimic bark texture

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits motionless on bark with legs spread wide, often positioned head-down on tree trunks - will remain perfectly still even when closely observed

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web for hunting - instead relies on ambush tactics, though may leave a thin silk dragline when moving between hunting spots

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with females noticeably larger than males - body feels solid and chunky compared to the more delicate build of orb weavers

habitat: Look for this spider on the bark of mature trees in mixed woodlands and forest edges throughout New England. It particularly favors rough-barked trees like oaks, maples, and hickories where its camouflage abilities work best. You'll most often spot them on tree trunks at eye level or slightly above, positioned where they can intercept flying insects.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often found sunning themselves on south-facing bark surfaces during cool mornings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both hunting behavior and color-changing abilities are most pronounced - this is the best time to observe their remarkable camouflage.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs, with females becoming more visible as they search for egg-laying sites in bark crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in deep bark crevices or under loose bark, becoming inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This spider can actually change its color over the course of several days by moving pigment granules within its skin cells - the same basic mechanism that allows chameleons to change color, but much slower and more deliberate.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bark-dwelling crab spiders, but the Multicolored Bark Crab Spider's ability to dramatically shift coloration and its preference for smooth-ish bark (rather than deeply furrowed bark) helps distinguish it. Remember: if it looks like it perfectly matches the bark and has that classic crab pose, you've likely found your spider.
contextualKnowledge: This species is quite rare in New England, with only a couple of confirmed sightings, so any observation would be noteworthy for local naturalists and citizen science projects. It's much more common in western North America, making New England sightings particularly special.
compareHints: Unlike its relative the Utah Crab Spider which prefers drier western habitats, the Multicolored Bark Crab Spider is adapted for the more humid conditions of eastern forests. Compared to other crab spiders in the Thomisidae family found in New England, it's unique in its strong association with bark rather than flowers or foliage, and its color-changing ability is more pronounced than most of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Utah Crab Spider differs from its close relative the Multicolored Bark Crab Spider by having more subdued, evenly mottled coloring rather than distinct color patches.
